subject: Goods and Services Tax
question_html: A "taxable event" under any tax law refers to:

options.A: Any transaction or occurrence that results in a tax consequence, and which determines the point at which tax would be levied
options.B: The date on which a taxpayer files its annual return
options.C: The rate of tax notified by the Government for a particular good or service
options.D: The office where a taxpayer is required to register

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Any transaction or occurrence that results in a tax consequence, and which determines the point at which tax would be levied

A taxable event is any transaction or occurrence that results in a tax consequence. It is the foundation stone of any taxation system, as it determines the point at which tax would be levied; before levying any tax, the taxable event needs to be ascertained.

subject: Goods and Services Tax
question_html: Under the earlier indirect tax regime, taxable events differed across statutes (e.g., manufacture, sale, rendering of service). GST resolves the resultant litigation by laying down:

options.B: One comprehensive taxable event, namely "Supply" - supply of goods or services or both
options.A: Multiple taxable events retained from the earlier regime, applied concurrently
options.C: "Manufacture" alone, retained from the erstwhile Central Excise law
options.D: "Sale" alone, retained from the erstwhile State VAT laws

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) One comprehensive taxable event, namely "Supply" - supply of goods or services or both

The GST law resolves the multiplicity-of-taxable-events problem by laying down one comprehensive taxable event, i.e. "Supply" of goods or services or both; earlier taxable events such as manufacture, sale, rendering of service, purchase, and entry into a territory of State have been done away with in favour of this single event.

options.A: Only actionable claims and nothing else

question_html: As per section 2(102) of the CGST Act, "services" means anything other than goods, money and securities, and specifically includes:

options.D: Activities relating to the use of money or its conversion by cash or by any other mode, from one form/currency/denomination to another, for which a separate consideration is charged, and also includes facilitating or arranging transactions in securities
options.A: Only the physical transportation of goods from one place to another

answer_html:

"Services" means anything other than goods, money and securities but includes activities relating to the use of money or its conversion by cash or by any other mode, from one form, currency or denomination, to another form, currency or denomination for which a separate consideration is charged; the expression "services" also includes facilitating or arranging transactions in securities [Section 2(102)].

subject: Goods and Services Tax
question_html: Which of the following is correctly excluded from the definition of "consideration" under section 2(31) of the CGST Act?

options.A: Any subsidy given by the Central Government or a State Government
options.B: Any payment made in money for the supply of goods or services
options.C: The monetary value of any act or forbearance in respect of the supply
options.D: Payment made by a person other than the recipient, for the supply

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Any subsidy given by the Central Government or a State Government

Consideration includes any payment made or to be made (whether in money or otherwise) and the monetary value of any act or forbearance, in respect of, in response to, or for the inducement of, the supply, whether by the recipient or by any other person, but shall not include any subsidy given by the Central Government or a State Government [Section 2(31)].

subject: Goods and Services Tax
question_html: As per section 2(31), a deposit given in respect of the supply of goods or services or both shall be considered as payment made for such supply:

options.B: Only if the supplier applies such deposit as consideration for the said supply
options.A: In every case, immediately upon receipt of the deposit by the supplier
options.C: Only if the deposit exceeds fifty thousand rupees
options.D: Never, regardless of how the supplier subsequently deals with the deposit

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Only if the supplier applies such deposit as consideration for the said supply

A deposit given in respect of the supply of goods or services or both shall not be considered as payment made for such supply unless the supplier applies such deposit as consideration for the said supply [Section 2(31)].

question_html: "Actionable claim" as defined under section 2(1) of the CGST Act (read with section 3 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882) means:

options.C: A claim to any debt (other than a debt secured by mortgage of immovable property or by hypothecation or pledge of movable property), or to any beneficial interest in movable property not in the possession of the claimant, which civil courts recognise as affording grounds for relief
options.A: A claim to any immovable property held in the actual possession of the claimant
options.B: A claim secured exclusively by a mortgage of immovable property
options.D: A claim that has already been decreed by a civil court and is no longer in dispute

Correct answer: (C) A claim to any debt (other than a debt secured by mortgage of immovable property or by hypothecation or pledge of movable property), or to any beneficial interest in movable property not in the possession of the claimant, which civil courts recognise as affording grounds for relief

"Actionable claim" means a claim to any debt, other than a debt secured by mortgage of immovable property or by hypothecation or pledge of movable property, or to any beneficial interest in movable property not in the possession, either actual or constructive, of the claimant, which the civil courts recognise as affording grounds for relief, whether such debt or beneficial interest be existent, accruing, conditional or contingent [Section 2(1) read with section 3 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882].

question_html: The provisions relating to the meaning and scope of "supply" are contained in section 7 of the CGST Act read with which Schedules?

options.D: Schedule I (activities treated as supply even without consideration), Schedule II (activities classified as supply of goods or supply of services) and Schedule III (activities treated neither as supply of goods nor supply of services)

options.A: An inclusive definition, which does not define the term exhaustively - clause (a) of sub-section (1) illustrates the forms of supply using the words "such as", making the list only illustrative and not exhaustive
options.B: An exhaustive, closed-list definition confined strictly to the eight forms of supply named in clause (a)

Section 7 is an inclusive definition and does not define the term "supply" exhaustively. Clause (a) of sub-section (1) illustrates the forms of supply, but the list is not exhaustive - this is further substantiated by the use of the words "such as" in the definition.

question_html: The meaning and scope of supply under section 7 can be understood, as a general rule, in terms of which three parameters?

options.C: Supply should be of goods or services; supply should be made for a consideration; and supply should be made in the course or furtherance of business
options.A: Supply should be of goods only; made for cash only; and made by a registered person only
options.B: Supply should be voluntary; made without consideration; and made outside the course of business

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Supply should be of goods or services; supply should be made for a consideration; and supply should be made in the course or furtherance of business

The meaning and scope of supply in terms of section 7 can generally be understood in terms of three parameters: (1) supply should be of goods or services, (2) supply should be made for a consideration, and (3) supply should be made in the course or furtherance of business.

question_html: Which statement best distinguishes "sale" from "transfer" as forms of supply under section 7(1)(a)?

options.B: In a sale, ownership of and title to property passes from one person to another for a price, whereas "transfer" (e.g., a company moving goods from its factory to its depot) may occur before any sale has actually taken place
options.A: Sale and transfer are legally identical terms and carry no distinction under GST
options.C: Transfer always requires a price to be paid, while sale never requires any price
options.D: Sale can only occur between related persons, while transfer can only occur between unrelated persons

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) In a sale, ownership of and title to property passes from one person to another for a price, whereas "transfer" (e.g., a company moving goods from its factory to its depot) may occur before any sale has actually taken place

The dictionary meaning of "sale" is the transfer of ownership of and title to property from one person to another for a price. "Transfer" (e.g., a company transferring goods from its factory to its depot for sale purposes) is "transfer" of goods where the sale has not yet taken place.

question_html: Which statement correctly distinguishes "barter" from "exchange" as forms of supply?

options.C: Barter deals with a transaction that only includes an exchange of goods/services for other goods/services (without using money), whereas exchange may cover a situation where the goods are paid for partly in goods and partly in money
options.A: Barter always involves money, while exchange never involves money
options.B: Exchange applies only to services, while barter applies only to goods
options.D: There is no practical difference; the CGST Act treats barter and exchange as legally interchangeable with identical scope

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Barter deals with a transaction that only includes an exchange of goods/services for other goods/services (without using money), whereas exchange may cover a situation where the goods are paid for partly in goods and partly in money

"Barter" is to exchange goods or services for other goods or services instead of using money, whereas "exchange" (per Black's Law Dictionary) is an act of giving or taking one thing for another and may cover a situation where the goods are paid for partly in goods and partly in money. Where there is a barter, the same activity constitutes both supply and consideration.

question_html: Under GST, licences, leases and rentals of goods with or without transfer of the right to use are covered under:

options.D: Supply of service, because there is no transfer of title in such supplies; such transactions are specifically treated as supply of service in Schedule II

Under GST, licences, leases and rentals of goods with or without transfer of the right to use are covered under the supply of service because there is no transfer of title in such supplies; such transactions are specifically treated as supply of service in Schedule II of the CGST Act.

subject: Goods and Services Tax
question_html: Bhushan donated a blackboard to Yoganisht Sansthan, a charitable yoga institution, which printed "Good wishes from Mr. Bhushan" underneath the donated blackboard. Applying Circular No. 116/35/2019 GST dated 11.10.2019, is there any supply of service by Yoganisht Sansthan to Bhushan?

options.A: No - since the acknowledgement is merely an expression of gratitude/public recognition and not advertisement of Bhushan's business, there is no quid pro quo and hence no supply of service for the donation
options.B: Yes - any acknowledgement of a donor's name automatically amounts to advertisement service, taxable under GST
options.C: Yes - all donations received by charitable institutions are consideration for supply, regardless of any acknowledgement
options.D: No - because charitable institutions are wholly exempt from being treated as "persons" under GST

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) No - since the acknowledgement is merely an expression of gratitude/public recognition and not advertisement of Bhushan's business, there is no quid pro quo and hence no supply of service for the donation

GST is not leviable on a donation where: (i) the payment has the character of a gift/donation made to a charitable organisation with a philanthropic purpose (i.e., no commercial gain), and (ii) the purpose is not advertisement. Since Yoganisht Sansthan's acknowledgement is not aimed at giving publicity/advertising Bhushan's business, there is no obligation (quid pro quo) on the institution to supply a service, and hence no GST liability [Circular No. 116/35/2019 GST dated 11.10.2019].

question_html: As per Circular No. 22/22/2017 GST dated 21.12.2017, when an artist sends artworks to a gallery merely for exhibition, is this a "supply"?

options.B: No - since no consideration flows from the gallery to the artist when the artworks are sent for exhibition; supply takes place, and GST becomes payable, only when a buyer actually selects and purchases a particular displayed artwork
options.A: Yes - the mere physical movement of the artworks to the gallery itself constitutes supply, regardless of any sale
options.C: Yes - galleries are always liable to pay GST on the full value of all artworks received for exhibition
options.D: No - artworks are permanently outside the scope of supply under GST, even when subsequently sold

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) No - since no consideration flows from the gallery to the artist when the artworks are sent for exhibition; supply takes place, and GST becomes payable, only when a buyer actually selects and purchases a particular displayed artwork

Artists give their work of art to galleries where it is exhibited for supply. It is only when a buyer selects a particular art work displayed at the gallery that the actual supply takes place [Circular No. 22/22/2017 GST dated 21.12.2017].

question_html: As per Circular No. 186/18/2022 GST dated 27.12.2022, can the deduction of "No Claim Bonus" (NCB) by an insurance company from the gross premium be regarded as consideration for a supply made by the insured to the insurer?

options.C: No - the insured is not under any contractual obligation to refrain from lodging an insurance claim in lieu of NCB; hence there is no supply by the insured to the insurance company, and NCB cannot be treated as consideration for any such supply
options.A: Yes - NCB represents consideration paid by the insurer for the insured's obligation to refrain from claiming, and is therefore taxable
options.B: Yes - but only where the NCB amount exceeds fifty thousand rupees in a financial year
options.D: No - because insurance companies are wholly outside the scope of GST

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) No - the insured is not under any contractual obligation to refrain from lodging an insurance claim in lieu of NCB; hence there is no supply by the insured to the insurance company, and NCB cannot be treated as consideration for any such supply

The customer/insured procures an insurance policy to indemnify himself against loss/injury as per the policy terms and is under no contractual obligation to refrain from claiming insurance in lieu of NCB. It is clarified that there is no supply by the insured to the insurance company in the form of agreeing to refrain from lodging a claim, and NCB cannot be considered consideration for any supply by the insured [Circular No. 186/18/2022 GST dated 27.12.2022].

subject: Goods and Services Tax
question_html: Which of the following statements about "consideration" under GST is correct?

options.D: Consideration need not always flow from the recipient of the supply - it can also be made by a third person, and it need not always be in the form of money
options.A: Consideration must always flow directly from the recipient of the supply and never from a third person
options.B: Consideration must always be in the form of money and can never be in kind
options.C: Consideration is irrelevant to determining whether a transaction is a supply under GST

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) Consideration need not always flow from the recipient of the supply - it can also be made by a third person, and it need not always be in the form of money

The dictionary meaning of "consideration" is payment, and it need not always be in the form of money - it can be in money or in kind, and covers anything which might possibly be done, given or made in exchange for something else. Further, a consideration need not always flow from the recipient of the supply - it can also be made by a third person.

question_html: Gautam, an artist, appoints Gambhir (an auctioneer) to auction his painting. question_html: As clarified vide Circular No. 92/11/2019 GST dated 07.03.2019, a "Buy One, Get One Free" offer (e.g., buy one soap and get one soap free) is best characterised, for GST purposes, as:

options.C: Not an individual supply of free goods, but a case of two or more individual supplies where a single price is charged for the entire supply - i.e., supplying two goods for the price of one, with taxability dependent on whether the supply is a composite supply or a mixed supply
options.A: An individual supply of one item at full price and one item entirely free of consideration and outside GST
options.B: A deemed supply under Schedule I, since one item is technically given without consideration
options.D: A transaction wholly outside the scope of supply since no separate price is charged for the "free" item

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Not an individual supply of free goods, but a case of two or more individual supplies where a single price is charged for the entire supply - i.e., supplying two goods for the price of one, with taxability dependent on whether the supply is a composite supply or a mixed supply

It may appear at first glance that in "Buy One, Get One Free" offers, one item is supplied free of cost without consideration. In fact, it is not an individual supply of free goods but a case of two or more individual supplies where a single price is charged for the entire supply - i.e., supplying two goods for the price of one. Taxability depends on whether the supply is a composite supply or a mixed supply [Circular No. 92/11/2019 GST dated 07.03.2019].

question_html: Section 7(1)(aa), read with its explanation, brings activities/transactions between a person (other than an individual) and its members or constituents, for consideration, within the ambit of "supply". This provision, in effect:

options.D: Overrules the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in State of West Bengal v. Calcutta Club Limited, which had held that transactions between a club and its members cannot be taxed owing to the doctrine of mutuality (a person cannot make a profit from himself), by deeming such person and its members/constituents to be two separate persons
options.A: Codifies and reaffirms the doctrine of mutuality, exempting all club-member transactions from GST
options.B: Applies only to transactions between a company and its shareholders, and to no other association or club
options.C: Has no relationship whatsoever to the doctrine of mutuality or the Calcutta Club Limited judgment

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) Overrules the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in State of West Bengal v. Calcutta Club Limited, which had held that transactions between a club and its members cannot be taxed owing to the doctrine of mutuality (a person cannot make a profit from himself), by deeming such person and its members/constituents to be two separate persons

The explanation to section 7(1)(aa) clarifies that such person (association, club, etc.) and its members or constituents shall be deemed to be two separate persons and the supply of activities or transactions between them shall be deemed to take place from one such person to another. This explanation, having an overriding, non-obstante effect, prevents the application of the doctrine of mutuality and effectively overrules the Supreme Court's judgment in State of West Bengal v. Calcutta Club Limited.

question_html: Under the Pagadi system prevalent in some States, a tenant acquires tenancy rights against payment of a tenancy premium, and may later transfer such tenancy rights to a new tenant against consideration. As clarified by CBIC, the transfer of tenancy rights against consideration:

options.D: Is squarely covered under supply of service liable to GST, as a form of lease or renting of property under Para 2 of Schedule II - it is not treated as sale of land/building under Schedule III merely because stamp duty and registration charges have also been levied on the transaction

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) Is squarely covered under supply of service liable to GST, as a form of lease or renting of property under Para 2 of Schedule II - it is not treated as sale of land/building under Schedule III merely because stamp duty and registration charges have also been levied on the transaction

The activity of transfer of tenancy right against consideration (tenancy premium) is squarely covered under supply of service liable to GST, being a form of lease or renting of property under Para 2 of Schedule II. question_html: As clarified vide Circular No. 178/10/2022 GST dated 03.08.2022, where "liquidated damages" are paid purely to compensate the aggrieved party for injury, loss or damage suffered due to breach of contract, with no agreement (express or implied) by the aggrieved party to tolerate the breach in exchange:

options.A: Such liquidated damages are merely a flow of money from the party causing the breach to the party suffering the loss, and do not constitute consideration for a supply of "tolerating an act"; hence they are not taxable
options.B: Such liquidated damages always constitute consideration for the supply of tolerating the breach of contract, and are taxable
options.C: Liquidated damages are treated as a mixed supply along with the underlying contract
options.D: Liquidated damages are treated as supply of goods under Para 4 of Schedule II

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Such liquidated damages are merely a flow of money from the party causing the breach to the party suffering the loss, and do not constitute consideration for a supply of "tolerating an act"; hence they are not taxable

The circular clarifies that liquidated damages cannot be said to be consideration received for tolerating the breach or non-performance of a contract - they are rather payments for not tolerating the breach. Where the amount is paid only to compensate for injury/loss/damage, with no agreement (express or implied) to refrain from or tolerate an act, such payments are merely a flow of money and are not taxable [Circular No. 178/10/2022 GST dated 03.08.2022].

question_html: As clarified vide Circular No. 243/37/2024 GST dated 31.12.2024, where a voucher qualifies as a Pre-paid Instrument (PPI) recognised by the RBI, transactions in such vouchers are treated as transactions in "money" and are excluded from the definition of goods/services; where a voucher instead creates an obligation on the supplier to accept it as consideration/part consideration (and is not a PPI), it is treated as an "actionable claim" and:

options.D: Transactions in the voucher itself are considered neither a supply of goods nor a supply of services, since actionable claims other than specified actionable claims fall under Entry 6 of Schedule III - though supply of the underlying goods/services for which the voucher is redeemed may still be taxable

question_html: Under Circular No. 243/37/2024 GST dated 31.12.2024, where distributors/sub-distributors (DSDs) purchase vouchers at a discounted rate from the voucher issuer and sell them onward (retaining full ownership and control throughout, on a Principal-to-Principal basis), the trading margin earned by such DSDs:

options.A: Amounts to trading of vouchers and is not leviable to GST as per section 9(1), since the DSDs own the vouchers outright and are not acting as an agent of the voucher issuer
options.B: Is treated as a commission/fee for a supply of agency services to the voucher issuer, and is leviable to GST
options.C: Is treated as supply of goods, since vouchers physically change hands between the DSD and the sub-distributor
options.D: Is always exempt from GST regardless of the basis (Principal-to-Principal or Principal-Agent) on which the vouchers are distributed

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Amounts to trading of vouchers and is not leviable to GST as per section 9(1), since the DSDs own the vouchers outright and are not acting as an agent of the voucher issuer

Where distributors/sub-distributors (DSDs) purchase vouchers at a discounted rate and sell them onward, retaining full ownership and control of the vouchers throughout (Principal-to-Principal basis), their trading margin (selling price minus acquisition cost) is not leviable to GST as per section 9(1), since it merely reflects trading of vouchers. This is distinct from Distributor/Sub-distributor Agents (DSAs), who act as agents of the voucher issuer and whose commission/fees are treated as a taxable supply of services to the voucher issuer.

subject: Goods and Services Tax
question_html: Which of the following is NOT listed among the indicators typically used to determine whether services are "naturally bundled" in the ordinary course of business?

options.B: The different elements of the bundle are separately available for purchase at freely negotiable, independent prices from the same supplier
options.A: There is a single price, or the customer pays the same amount, no matter how much of the package is actually received or used
options.C: The elements are normally advertised as a package, and the different elements are not available separately
options.D: The different elements are integral to one overall supply, such that removing one or more would affect the nature of the supply

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) The different elements of the bundle are separately available for purchase at freely negotiable, independent prices from the same supplier

Indicators of natural bundling include: a single price regardless of how much of the package is used; the elements being advertised as a package; the different elements not being available separately; and the elements being integral to one overall supply such that removing one affects its nature. Elements being separately available at independent prices is, if anything, an indicator AGAINST natural bundling.

question_html: A 5-star hotel is booked for a conference of 100 delegates on a lump sum package including accommodation, breakfast, tea/coffee during the conference, access to a fitness room, the conference room and business centre facilities. If the principal service is judged to be "convention service", how is the composite supply taxed?

options.D: The principal service (convention service) is able to capture the entire essence of the package, and the composite supply is charged to tax accordingly at the rate applicable to convention service, applied to the entire package value
options.A: Each of the bundled services (accommodation, breakfast, fitness room, etc.) must compulsorily be taxed separately at its own respective rate, since a hotel booking can never be a composite supply
options.B: The package must always be taxed at the highest of the individual applicable rates, since it is a mixed supply and not a composite supply
options.C: GST cannot be levied on any part of the package, since business conferences are outside the scope of supply

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) The principal service (convention service) is able to capture the entire essence of the package, and the composite supply is charged to tax accordingly at the rate applicable to convention service, applied to the entire package value

As is evident, a bouquet of services is provided, many chargeable at different effective rates. If the principal service is described as convention service, it captures the entire essence of the package, and the composite supply may be charged to tax accordingly at the rate applicable to that principal service, applied to the entire package value. (It remains open to the hotel to charge individually for the services, as long as there is no attempt to offload the value of one service onto another chargeable at a concessional rate.)

question_html: As per Circular No. 34/8/2018-GST dated 01.03.2018, in retreading of tyres (where the pre-dominant element is the process of retreading and the rubber used is an ancillary supply), this composite supply is classified as:

options.A: Supply of service, since retreading is a process applied to the customer's own tyre and the process is the pre-dominant element
options.B: Supply of goods, since a physical rubber component (new tread) is added to the tyre
options.C: A mixed supply, since retreading involves both a service element and a goods element sold together for a single price
options.D: Supply of goods, but only where the old tyre belongs to the supplier of the retreaded tyre

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Supply of service, since retreading is a process applied to the customer's own tyre and the process is the pre-dominant element

As per Circular No. 34/8/2018-GST dated 01.03.2018, in retreading of tyres, which is a composite supply, the pre-dominant element is the process of retreading, which is a supply of service; the rubber used for retreading is an ancillary supply. question_html: As per Circular No. 201/13/2023 GST dated 01.08.2023, where the sale of a cinema ticket and supply of food/beverages are clubbed together and the bundled supply satisfies the test of a composite supply, the entire bundled supply is taxed:

options.B: At the rate applicable to the principal supply, i.e., the service of exhibition of cinema

options.C: As a mixed supply, at the highest of the cinema ticket rate and the restaurant service rate
options.D: Separately - cinema ticket at the cinema rate and food/beverages at the restaurant rate, in every case regardless of bundling

answer_html:

case_facts_html: Vaidik Enterprises has a registered factory in Pune, Maharashtra and a registered depot in Nashik, Maharashtra (separate GST registration obtained for the depot, though both are within the same State). During the year: (i) Vaidik Enterprises transfers finished goods worth ₹8,00,000 from its Pune factory to its Nashik depot without charging any consideration, so that the goods can be sold from the depot; (ii) Vaidik Enterprises permanently disposes of an old delivery van (on which full input tax credit had been availed at the time of purchase) to a scrap dealer, free of cost; and (iii) Vaidik Enterprises' proprietor gifts a laptop worth ₹35,000 (used in the business, on which ITC had been availed) to his son on his birthday, from the business's stock, without any consideration and unconnected with any employer-employee relationship.
question_html: Is the transfer of finished goods worth ₹8,00,000 from the Pune factory to the Nashik depot, without consideration, a "supply"?

options.C: Yes - since the factory and depot hold separate GST registrations, they are "distinct persons" under section 25(4); supply of goods between distinct persons, in the course or furtherance of business, is deemed to be supply under Para 2 of Schedule I even without consideration
options.A: No - since both establishments are located within the same State of Maharashtra
options.B: No - since no consideration is charged for the stock transfer
options.D: Yes, but only because the goods are being transferred for eventual sale and not for any other purpose

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Yes - since the factory and depot hold separate GST registrations, they are "distinct persons" under section 25(4); supply of goods between distinct persons, in the course or furtherance of business, is deemed to be supply under Para 2 of Schedule I even without consideration

As per section 25(4), a person who has obtained more than one registration, whether within the same State/UT or in different States/UTs, is treated as a distinct person in respect of each such registration. Since Vaidik Enterprises has obtained separate registrations for its Pune factory and Nashik depot, they are distinct persons, and the stock transfer between them (in the course or furtherance of business) is deemed to be supply under Para 2 of Schedule I, even without consideration.

question_html: Is the gift of the ₹35,000 business laptop (ITC availed) by the proprietor to his son a "supply", and does the ₹50,000 employer-employee gift exemption under the proviso to Para 2 of Schedule I apply to this gift?

options.A: It qualifies as supply under Para 1 of Schedule I (permanent transfer of a business asset on which ITC has been availed); however, the ₹50,000 proviso exemption under Para 2 does NOT apply here, because that proviso is specific to gifts by an employer to an employee, and the proprietor's son is neither an employee of the business nor a "distinct/related person" transaction covered by that proviso
options.B: It is not a supply at all, since the value of the laptop (₹35,000) is below ₹50,000, and the proviso to Para 2 of Schedule I exempts it
options.C: It is not a supply, since gifts by a proprietor to a family member are always outside the scope of GST
options.D: It is a supply only if the son subsequently resells the laptop for consideration

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) It qualifies as supply under Para 1 of Schedule I (permanent transfer of a business asset on which ITC has been availed); however, the ₹50,000 proviso exemption under Para 2 does NOT apply here, because that proviso is specific to gifts by an employer to an employee, and the proprietor's son is neither an employee of the business nor a "distinct/related person" transaction covered by that proviso

The proviso to Para 2 of Schedule I exempting gifts up to ₹50,000 in a financial year applies specifically to gifts by an employer to an employee - the proprietor's son is not an employee. Instead, this transaction is properly analysed under Para 1 of Schedule I: permanent transfer/disposal of a business asset (the laptop, on which ITC has been availed), without consideration, is deemed supply regardless of its value or the recipient's identity.

question_html: Does Balaraam qualify as an "agent" of Naidu Traders under Para 3 of Schedule I for supply of goods?

options.B: No - Balaraam is only acting as a procurement agent and has in no way involved himself in the supply or receipt of the goods; since the supplier issues the invoice directly to Naidu Traders (and not through Balaraam), Balaraam is not an agent for supply of goods under Para 3 of Schedule I
options.A: Yes - any person who identifies suppliers on behalf of a principal automatically becomes an agent under Para 3
options.C: Yes - since Balaraam receives a fee for his procurement services, he necessarily falls under Para 3 of Schedule I
options.D: No - because raw cotton is an agricultural product and is therefore outside the scope of Para 3 of Schedule I altogether

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) No - Balaraam is only acting as a procurement agent and has in no way involved himself in the supply or receipt of the goods; since the supplier issues the invoice directly to Naidu Traders (and not through Balaraam), Balaraam is not an agent for supply of goods under Para 3 of Schedule I

options.C: Yes, since the sale value (₹40,000) exceeds the registration threshold applicable to Nishtha
options.D: No, because two-wheelers are specifically excluded from the definition of "goods" under GST

question_html: How is Ranjhana Appliances' supply of the refrigerator with mandatory warranty and free maintenance visits, for a single invoice price, classified?

options.B: Mixed supply - taxed at the highest of the rates applicable to the refrigerator, warranty and maintenance components
options.C: Three entirely independent supplies, each to be taxed separately at its own rate
options.D: Neither a composite nor a mixed supply, since warranty services are not "supplies" under GST at all

question_html: How is Chakori Retail's pre-paid, RBI-recognised gift instrument treated for GST purposes when it is issued or transacted?

options.D: It falls under the definition of "money" (being a Pre-paid Instrument/PPI recognised by the RBI), and is accordingly excluded from the definitions of both goods and services; transactions in it are not supply, though the subsequent redemption for actual goods/services may attract GST on those goods/services
options.A: It is treated as an "actionable claim" under Entry 6 of Schedule III, and its transfer is a non-supply on that basis
options.B: It is treated as supply of goods at the time of issuance, taxed on its full stored value
options.C: It is treated as a mixed supply comprising money plus a service of stored-value management

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) It falls under the definition of "money" (being a Pre-paid Instrument/PPI recognised by the RBI), and is accordingly excluded from the definitions of both goods and services; transactions in it are not supply, though the subsequent redemption for actual goods/services may attract GST on those goods/services

As clarified vide Circular No. 243/37/2024 GST dated 31.12.2024, a Pre-paid Instrument (PPI) recognised by the RBI falls under the definition of "money" and is excluded from the definitions of goods and services - distinct from a voucher that is merely an "actionable claim". Transactions in a PPI-type voucher are accordingly not supply, though supply of the underlying goods/services obtained on redemption may separately attract GST.

Para 2 of Schedule II specifically lists "any lease, tenancy, easement, licence to occupy land" as supply of services.
